articles.title: Behind China's spectacular rise, voices who defied it say they are being drowned out
articles.summary: China's immense clout now also has the flex of soft power. Critics and dissidents say their voices are being drowned out.
articles.full_text:
Image source, Getty Images Image caption, 
China's economic might is drowning out our voices, say activists and dissidents By Kelly Ng 
- Published 4 hours ago 
For Uyghur activist Dolkun Isa, who has lived in exile in Germany for nearly three decades, the thinning of the crowds is the clearest measure of how much his cause is slipping off the world's radar. 
"Back in 2018, we could easily get thousands of people out in the streets to protest against China's human rights violations. Nowadays, we have trouble finding even 500." 
It was in 2018 that reports emerged that China had detained up to a million Uyghurs and other Muslims in mass internment camps in its north-western province of Xinjiang. Beijing, which said the camps were for "re-education" to counter separatist violence, denied the allegations detailing alarming rights abuses. 
But an international outcry, including protests, followed. Western governments rolled out trade bans and sanctions against senior Chinese officials, and froze their assets, and at least nine countries issued parliamentary resolutions condemning the detentions. 
It was a time "when we felt the world was finally listening", says Dolkun, 59, who served as president of the Munich-based World Uyghur Congress from 2017-2024 . 
But today, "we find ourselves competing against economic interests and geopolitical calculations to capture the world's attention. For me, this is one of the most painful aspects of our struggle". 
Image source, Dolkun Isa Image caption, 
Uyghur activist Dolkun Isa has lived in exile in Germany for nearly three decades 
Few corners of the world remain untouched by China's rise. Its electric vehicles pack highways from Brazil to Belgium, made-in-China batteries, solar panels, AI models and microdramas fuel daily consumption in so many places, and Labubu dolls , Pop Mart's furry gap-toothed plush, dangle from backpacks almost everywhere. 
China's immense economic clout now also has the flex of soft power , drowning out voices that say their fight against the Communist Party cannot compete with the country's gleaming skylines, advanced exports or futuristic ambitions. 
Buoyed by its successes, Beijing is also swapping the "stick" for the "carrot", says Uyghur journalist Arslan Hidayat, who was born and raised in Australia, where he runs Kashgar Times. 
Activists tell the BBC Beijing has been offering family reunions, money and the promise of safety - in return, they are asked for information about their networks and to promote pro-party narratives. The result, activists say, is a movement with fewer voices and less trust. 
The Chinese embassy in the UK dismissed the activists' claims that they would be asked to spy on or disclose information about fellow exiles. 
Image source, Getty Images Image caption, 
Sheznhen, a rich, buzzing city on the soth-eastern coast, has emerged as one of China's star attractions for tech and tourism 
China's "economic muscle" has earned it respect abroad and reshaped foreign policy, says Ian Johnson, a Pulitzer Prize-winning journalist who has long reported on Chinese civil society. 
"At the same time, Western governments have become much more inwardly focused and populist, pushing human rights down their lists of priorities." 
China's human rights record has not earned a mention in any of the three summits Xi Jinping and US President Donald Trump held this year, including the one in Shenzhen last week. As Beijing's leverage on the global stage has grown, so has the cost of confrontation or condemnation. 
This shift in Beijing's image and tactics is deeply worrying, dissidents say, because it is weakening both their networks and the international pressure they hope to build. 
In July Tibetan activist Lobga Rangzen died after he set himself on fire outside the UN headquarters in New York. He was protesting against China's sweeping new "ethnic unity law" which, among other things, requires minorities, including Tibetans, to learn Mandarin. The UN called it an "absolutely tragic" incident, but attention quickly faded. 
His death was "an appeal to the international community", says Tenzin Dorjee, a researcher at the Tibet Action Institute, but he thinks much of the world is reluctant to criticise China because of the power it wields. 
That same month Dolkun tried to rally supporters against the same law but he met with a muted response. 
"Many people have dialled down on their activism over the years because they are thinking about their loved ones back in China," Dolkun says. 
Image source, Getty Images Image caption, 
Donald Trump and Xi Jinping have held three summits so far this year 
Arslan says he has interviewed at least a dozen Uyghur exiles who were "invited to go back to China on the condition that they would provide information to Chinese agents from time to time". 
The questions seem "fairly innocuous", he adds: "Who lives around you? Which Uyghur restaurants do you frequent? We believe these are used to build out the profiles of dissidents overseas." 
Beijing's embassy in the UK said in its response to the BBC that "facilitating visits to China by overseas Chinese to reunite with their families" is a "normal part" of consular services. 
"China respects and protects the lawful rights and interests of people of all ethnic groups, including the Uyghurs, and their freedom to maintain contact with family members overseas," it added. 
These family visits often happen in large groups and are well documented on China's official platforms. 
In Turkey, which hosts tens of thousands of Muslim minorities from Xinjiang, Chinese Consul-General Wei Xiaodong was photographed sending off some 30 participants from Istanbul in January. 
Image source, Chinese Consulate General in Istanbul's WeChat account Image caption, 
Consul-General Wei Xiaodong (in the red scarf) pictured sending people off in January 
"He expressed hope that the diaspora returning to Xinjiang would experience the region's development... and would actively promote these developments upon their return to Turkey," read a post on the consulate's WeChat page. 
Beijing has repackaged Xinjiang into a traveller's haven. The region saw more than 300 million domestic and international tourist visits last year, more than double the number in 2018, Chinese authorities say. 
The post from China's Turkish consulate concluded with a clip showing loved ones hugging and presenting bouquets as they reunite with family at the airport in Urumqi, the capital of Xinjiang. 
"People are happy to stay quiet and lay low for the little communication they've been allowed to establish with their loved ones," Arslan says. 
Though the trips are publicised, it is unclear what makes someone eligible to participate in them. Some suggest that even dating histories come under the microscope. 
Alim*, a Uyghur exiled in Turkey, says a friend who made an appeal to the consulate to consider her for a trip was rejected, with staffers alluding to her past relationship with a Kazakh man who at one point was "quite active" in lobbying for his parents who were detained in China. 
"She was very eager to go on one of these 'family visits' because she hasn't seen her loved ones back home in so many years... She was crushed that she was rejected," says Alim. 
"The way I understand it, the 'ideal participant' is someone influential enough to amplify China's messages, yet not associated with anything or anyone too political." 
Image source, Getty Images Image caption, 
Xinjiang has been sold as an exotic destination, bringing in huge numbers of tourists 
When Mehmut* was invited on a family visit in October 2024, he jumped at the opportunity. 
The Uyghur businessman hoped a trip back to China would help him re-establish the links needed to "keep our business afloat". Far from the warm reunions Mehmut had expected, he says his engagement with friends and family "felt superficial". 
"It was not like officials were actively monitoring me or restricting my movements. But there was a great dose of fear and self-censorship in my conversations with people," he says. 
"Some were caught off guard to see me return, others appeared very cautious with what they told me. The experience just made me feel very uncomfortable." 
These visits do not just serve Beijing's narrative; they also drive a wedge within communities, activists say. 
Abduweli Ayup, a prominent Uyghur linguist based in Norway, has observed former activists going off the grid after returning from these trips. 
"Some have deleted their social media accounts and cut off contact with us," he says. "Others appear to be suspicious of us or concerned that what we were doing would compromise theirs or their families' safety." 
The fact that only a few get selected to visit the homeland "creates confusion within the diaspora," says Tibetan activist Karma Rinchen. 
"They get sidelined when they return... Very sadly, our suspicions that some of them are feeding information back to the Chinese authorities have turned out to be true." 
Image source, Karma Rinchen Image caption, 
Karma Rinchen's parents were among thousands who fled Tibet alongside the Dalai Lama in 1959 
Rinchen serves as information secretary in the Tibetan government-in-exile in the northern Indian town of Dharamshala. His parents were among thousands who followed their spiritual leader Dalai Lama into exile after China annexed Tibet. 
Over the decades, waves of others have fled Chinese rule seeking greater freedom or asylum from Beijing's crackdowns - dissidents and student activists in the wake of the Tiannanmen Square massacre; lawyers, journalists, purged officials and critics in the years after, and, more recently, Hong Kong saw a steady exodus build as the pro-democracy movement was crushed. 
Many have kept on fighting. But now, they say, Beijing's might is chipping away at their struggle, making it ever harder to stand up to the Chinese Communist Party. 
"Many among us have been separated from our families for generations and are eager to set foot on Tibet soil," Rinchen says. "This is exactly the kind of desperation the Communist Party seeks to target." 
But he adds this only means communities have to "work harder to make sure their voices are heard". 
Image source, AFP via Getty Images Image caption, 
A memorial for Tibetan activist Lobga Rangzen who set himself on fire outside the UN headquarters in New York 
"For Tibetans, this is not something we can simply walk away from. Our struggle is about our identity, our culture, our religion and the basic rights of our people. We have been doing this work for many decades, and we have learned to remain patient and persistent," Rinchen adds. 
For many, that persistence continues to be tested on a personal level. 
Uyghur musician Mirkamel Tourghoun has lived as a refugee in Paris since 2008, spending most of his time writing music and making films about Uyghur culture. 
The 42-year-old has chosen the painful path of cutting off contact with his family who remain in Urumqi. 
In January, he received a call from someone claiming to be an official from the city. 
"What if we get rid of all this [political] pressure, and allow you to return and see your parents? Do you have such plans?" the caller asked. 
"What's happened in the past is in the past. You should turn a new page. The pen is in your own hand." 
The official claimed his father was gravely ill and that time was running out to see him. "It's emotional blackmail," Mirkamel says. 
He declined the official's invitation: "Tell my family to forget they ever had a child like me. There is no other solution." 
* Name changed on request to protect interviewee's identity

articles.title: A renovation was meant to improve these Hong Kong homes - it ended in a blaze that killed 168
articles.summary: A year after one of Hong Kong's deadliest fires, families left behind are still waiting for justice.
articles.full_text:
Figure caption, 
Watch: Christy says she still sends WhatsApp messages to her husband who died in the blaze By Grace Tsoi ,  BBC World Service ,  Phoebe Kong ,  BBC Chinese ,  Reporting from Hong Kong   and   Yvette Tan 
- Published 25 November 2026 
It was a sunny Wednesday afternoon on 26 November last year, and Mrs Lau was attending a dance class at an activity centre close to her home. 
At around 14:45 she heard the faint sounds of fire engine sirens - but didn't think much of it. 
It was only a while later, when she started receiving calls from a friend, that she found out that Wang Fuk Court - the eight-block apartment complex she had called home for the past 40 years - was ablaze. And her husband - a wheelchair user - was trapped inside their home. 
"I grabbed my things quickly and ran down without even putting my shoes on properly," Mrs Lau, who wanted to be identified only by her surname, told the BBC. 
When she got there, the building had been cordoned off by police. 
She called her 74-year-old husband but he told her not to worry - he hadn't heard an alarm so it was probably a small fire, he said. 
Mrs Lau could only watch helplessly as the blaze tore through Wang Fuk Court at a peak speed of about 10m (33ft) per second - an "unprecedented" rate, a final report released by an independent committee in relation to the deadly blaze that killed 168 people found. 
It was a tragedy that was entirely preventable but happened as a result of a series of human errors, fire safety failures, alleged fraud and suspected corruption, said the report. 
"It was ferocious… I saw the fire jump [from one building to another] - then a huge fireball burst. It was truly hell on Earth. How could anyone possibly escape?" said Mrs Lau. 
She tried calling her husband again. This time, there was no answer. 
The body of Lau Man Kwong was eventually found by rescuers - he had locked himself inside the toilet. 
"He was wearing his slippers, sitting on the toilet and clutching his identity card," said his wife, who added that she escaped death "by the narrowest margin". 
"I would have held onto my husband and died with him. 
"He was such a good person. I just don't understand why he had to die in such a terrible way." 
Mr Lau and his wife moved into Wang Fuk Court in 1983 - the year the building was completed. 
She recalls an idyllic life - a family with three children who were able to grow up close to the sea and spend weekends playing at a nearby park. 
"All three of my children adored my husband… He could be very stern, and I was the only woman who could make him laugh." 
Image source, Supplied Image caption, 
Lau Man Kwong took care of his grandson before his death (blurred at source) 
No way out 
In 2024, mandated renovations began in Wang Fuk Court. 
In Hong Kong, all buildings over 30 years old have to undergo an inspection - and any necessary renovations as a result. 
Like many building complexes in Hong Kong, Wang Fuk Court had a management committee that oversaw things like building repairs. As many as 57 construction companies submitted bids. But the company that won, Prestige Construction and Engineering (PC&E), submitted the most expensive bid at HK$336m ($42.8m; £32.4m). 
Residents, many of whom were over 65, had to bear the cost. The hefty bills triggered protests but eventually, the contract was signed. But once the renovations began in July 2024, residents were unhappy. 
Among the complaints was that workers constantly smoked on site, dropping cigarette butts everywhere. 
The 1,154 page report suggested the fire was caused by a lit cigarette. 
Image source, Reuters Image caption, 
The fire was one of Hong Kong's deadliest in decades 
There were also complaints about most of Wang Fuk Court's eight buildings having their windows taped over with foam boards to stop debris falling in - blocking daylight or any sort of view at all, for months. 
All eight buildings were also covered in a protective mesh netting and bamboo scaffolding. 
The report also found that after typhoons damaged the original scaffolding nets in 2025, cheaper non-fire-retardant replacements were chosen - something that was done as a "cost-saving measure at the expense of the safety of the residents". 
Residents had filed nearly 140 complaints to six government departments, including the fire services and the buildings departments, in and after 2024, but these were largely ignored, the report went on to say. 
It also revealed that a staff member of the estate's property manager, ISS, had turned off the power supply to the fire alarms in all eight buildings - which is why no alarms rang on the day itself. 
ISS later told the BBC it had "reviewed and reinforced its procedures [and] staff training" in Hong Kong, adding that it takes the findings of the report "very seriously". 
But for those who did manage to flee their homes - the emergency staircase turned out to be another death trap. Windows were removed from some fire escape stairwells to create temporary openings for workers - letting in smoke and cutting off vital escape routes. 
Dozens, including Christy's husband, died in such stairwells. 
Image source, Lam Yik / BBC Chinese Image caption, 
Christy's daughter celebrated her ninth birthday the day before the fire 
Christy, who wanted to be identified only by her first name, says her husband was at home alone when the fire broke out. She only found out about it when her friends sent her messages about it. By the time she made it to the apartment complex, it was already cordoned off. 
She found out later that he had died of smoke inhalation in the stairwell, something she says that is at least of some consolation to her. 
"My husband's body would have been burnt and he would have been in more pain if he was at home. At the very least… his suffering was minimal." 
Christy says her family had just celebrated their eldest child's ninth birthday the day before - they had saved some leftover cake in the fridge to eat the next day. Their father never got to eat it. 
Both children have been deeply affected by the loss of their father. 
Her youngest child, a seven-year-old boy, had "covered his ears and yelled" when he was first told what had happened to his father. 
He now often comforts his mother, saying he will take care of her as he is the only man in the family. 
"He hides his emotions. A seven-year-old child should not behave this way, and I feel heartbroken," says Christy, who has herself been diagnosed with PTSD and depression. 
Her daughter has "extreme thoughts" she says, and channels her emotions through art. 
She turned 10 on Wednesday, but this year, there was no birthday celebration in sight. 
Her birthday, she says, will now instead be a day to commemorate her father. 
Bid-rigging and rubber stamps 
Wang Fuk Court's problems date back to before the renovations began. 
The management company hired to oversee and supervise the project, Will Power, conspired with PC&E to defraud residents in Wang Fuk Court, according to the city's Independent Commission Against Corruption (ICAC). 
Although PC&E was found to have breached safety requirements and violated building department rules for multiple previous projects, homeowners at Wang Fuk Court were told that they had a clean record. 
The ICAC alleges that this was part of a lucrative scheme, with Will Power's director Wong Hap-yin, along with other individuals, laundering over $5m in suspected proceeds from the tendering process from Wang Fuk Court, among other housing projects. 
Once PC&E cinched the contract, Will Power's registered inspector - an individual meant to oversee the renovations - merely rubber-stamped the documents, without having actually conducted any inspections personally, the report added. 
Will Power has been since liquidated and PC&E could not be reached for a response. 
Both companies - Will Power and PC&E - and seven individuals have been charged with 25 counts of offences including manslaughter, conspiracy to defraud, attempting to pervert the course of public justice and tax evasion. 
Four of them are still in custody but none of the cases have gone to trial yet. 
The report said both companies involved were the "main culprits responsible". 
But it also directed heavy criticism at authorities, saying that "no government department took effective ownership of various fire safety issues and complaints about fire hazards fell into a vacuum". 
One expert, Prof John Burns of Hong Kong University, had called the tragedy the "largest governance crisis" that authorities have faced since 2020 - a reference to the controversial National Security Law that was passed in that year. 
On the day the report was released, almost one year after the fire, Hong Kong's housing chief Winnie Ho resigned and the city's top leader John Lee apologised for the first time, promising that a "large number" of reforms would be rolled out. 
Image source, Getty Images Image caption, 
Homeowners at Wang Fuk Court (pictured) were told their construction company had a clean record 
A shell of a home 
Five months after the fire, Mrs Lau was allowed into her flat for the first time to collect any personal belongings that might have remained. 
In her first visit, she was given just three hours to retrieve 40 years' worth of belongings. 
Pictures taken from the visit show a home that has been utterly burned out - with every surface blackened and soot covering the floor. 
"I almost fainted when I saw what had become of my home. I don't understand how the home I had built, such a warm and beautiful home, could end up like this," said Mrs Lau. 
Image source, Supplied Image caption, 
The frame of Mr Lau's wheelchair was one of the few things left in their burnt home 
Her children, who came with her, described the house as a "war zone". Among the rubble, they found broken pieces of a piggy bank that Mr Lau had dutifully filled with coins every day for the past 20 years. 
"Everyone in our family knew it was his favourite possession. The piggy bank died with him," said Mrs Lau. 
Mrs Lau and her daughter have since rented a place nearby to live - and she is worried about how she is going to afford a new house. 
The government has said it will spend $867m (£663m) to acquire affected flats - but Mrs Lau says it is not nearly enough to buy a similarly sized flat in the area. 
Still, her family was in a better position than many others, she said. 
"Should I say that we are fortunate? 
"I lost my husband but many families lost multiple family members... Babies less than a year old died. " 
Stories have emerged of some of the other victims - a six-month-old who died alongside her 68-year-old grandmother when the fire broke out. 
The bodies of an Indonesian domestic helper and the elderly person she worked for were found huddled together. 
Image source, BBC Chinese / Phoebe Kong Image caption, 
Mrs Lau's son has since bought new piggy banks in memory of his father 
As for Christy, she says she is planning to file a lawsuit against those responsible for the fire - but acknowledges that even if she wins, she "can't [get] my husband's life back". 
"I share things that happen in our daily life, as if he still existed," she says. "I often write to him, 'I miss you so much. Are you doing well on the other side?'" 
It's a similar story for Mrs Lau, who says she can't go anywhere without seeing her husband. 
"Every day, something reminds me of him," she said. 
"I still find it very hard to accept that my husband is gone, my home is gone, and so many of my neighbours are gone…. This place was my roots. I never imagined it would also mark an ending for me."

articles.title: US announces new tariffs on host of countries including China
articles.summary: The new levies would hit many of America's biggest trading partners, including China and the EU.
articles.full_text:
Figure caption, 
Watch: What we know about Trump's Thanksgiving tariffs By Michael Race ,  Jonathan Josephs   and   Osmond Chia ,  Business reporters 
- Published 25 November 2026 Updated 26 November 2026 
The US has announced a fresh raft of tariffs as President Donald Trump pushes ahead with his signature trade policy. 
The new taxes charged on imports to America are set to hit many of the country's biggest trading partners - China, the European Union and 12 other jurisdictions, including Japan, South Korea and Taiwan. 
The White House began investigating the trade practices of other countries in March after the US Supreme Court ruled Trump's previously announced Liberation Day tariffs were illegal . 
China is facing the highest tariff rate of up to 40%, followed by Vietnam at up to 35%, with others facing either 20% or 25%. 
The US Trade Representative (USTR) announced the proposed tariffs together with extensive reports of how each jurisdiction's trade practices purportedly impact American commerce. 
The new duties are not expected to take effect until next year and have to go through rounds of public consultation and, potentially, hearings. 
Tariffs are taxes levied on imported goods. The amount is typically calculated as a percentage of a good's value and paid to the government by businesses importing products. 
Some of these rates will be effectively reduced because of caps on tariffs Trump has agreed to. Individual countries also face different levies. 
The proposed tariffs will affect goods from China, the European Union, Singapore, Switzerland, Indonesia, Malaysia, Cambodia, Thailand, Korea, Vietnam, Taiwan, Bangladesh, Japan, and India. 
The USTR's Jamieson Greer said the latest tariffs issued would "level the playing field for American workers and chart a new, more sustainable course for the world economy". 
Image source, Bloomberg via Getty Images Image caption, 
Jamieson Greer, US trade representative 
He said that many of America's trading partners had "for decades" adopted industrial strategies which included "targeting manufacturing, wage and labor suppression". 
They also employ "other market distorting practices that tilt the trade balance in their favour while eroding America's manufacturing base", Greer said. 
But economists have warned tariffs can fuel inflation and push prices up for consumers if businesses pass on higher costs, as well as dampen global trade. 
Trump has repeatedly threatened or imposed tariffs during his second term, arguing they will boost US manufacturing and create jobs. 
Despite a poor result for the Republican party in the midterm elections, the president has continued to press on with his flagship trade policy. 
Trump is also seeking to cut the US trade deficit - the gap between the value of goods it buys from other countries and those it sells to them. 
Image source, Getty Images Image caption, 
Trump's so-called Liberation Day tariffs were struck down by the Supreme Court earlier this year 
These new levies are build on a "stronger legal foundation" under US law compared with Trump's April 2025 Liberation Day tariffs, Singapore Management University economics lecturer Chang Pao-Li said. 
Trump previously invoked emergency presidential powers to impose tariffs that have since been struck down, while his latest approach relies on the USTR's authority to impose tariffs to address certain foreign trade practices, she said. 
The levies are still likely to face legal challenges, but there has been a "historical precedent" for such tariffs remaining in force, Chang said. 
Many tariffs imposed under Section 301 - a law that allows the US to probe and retaliate against foreign trade practices - during Trump's first term remained in effect during his successor Joe Biden's administration. 
However, Stephen Brown, chief North America economist for Capital Economics, said the latest tariff announcement was "not as alarming as it looks", due to the taxes "essentially replacing" previously announced tariffs made in the summer. 
"The increase in the effective tariff rate looks set to be a touch lower than we've been assuming for our forecasts, although the new tariffs will still provide a marginal boost to prices," he said in a note. 
The additional tariff burden is likely to be small because a limited number of goods are subject to the new duties, Brown added. 
Jurisdictions affected by the new wave of tariffs have voiced their disapproval over the Trump administration's move. 
Washington has also proposed a 10% tariff on goods from Brazil, as part of a separate investigation over what it says are "harmful trade practices" undercutting American workers. 
Brazilian authorities expressed their "outrage" at the announcement, saying that the move is aimed at pressuring the government to change regulations around issues like digital trade. 
The South American nation faces duties on finished aircraft and sugar sold to the US. 
"Brazil will not yield to such threats," President Luiz Inacio Lula da Silva's office said. 
The European Commission rejected the new US tariffs, saying it would investigate the reasons for bringing them in. It pointed out that tariffs are limited to the 15% previously agreed. 
The latest tariff rate is "not consistent" with the reality of bilateral economic-trade cooperation between the US and Vietnam, Vietnamese Deputy Prime Minister Bui Thanh Son said. 
The Japanese government said the US tariffs were "regrettable", while the Singapore government said it disagrees with the White House's findings and that it is engaging the USTR to explore ways to reduce the tariff. 
South Korea's trade minister said the proposed 15% tariff will be "more than a decent outcome" as it would fall in line with a previously agreed limit with Washington. 
Last year, Seoul pledged $350bn (£267bn) in US investments in exchange for lower tariffs as part of a trade deal.

- Published 1 August 2025

- Published 19 October 
US trading partners have been "waiting for this shoe to drop" and have argued that they are being wrongly accused of producing too much, said the Asia Society Policy Institute's Wendy Cutler, a former senior US trade negotiator. 
"Many believe that China, not them, should be the target for US action," she added. 
Chinese Foreign Ministry spokesperson Guo Jiakun described the new tariffs as a form of "political manipulation", describing as "false" the US claim that China produces more than it can consume. 
The tariff announcement is likely to increase tensions between the US and China, the world's two biggest economies, who remain locked in a trade dispute and the AI race. 
The two countries have also been embroiled in a tit-for-tat tariffs war, which is currently on hold. 
Despite last week's meeting between Trump and China's President Xi Jinping, the two sides made no announcement on the trade war truce, which is set to expire on 10 January. 
Beijing has remained vague on how it will respond but for now seems "prepared to live with the new rates provided they don't exceed 20%", Cutler said.

articles.title: Xi's anti-corruption campaign ensnares rising star in Chinese Communist Party
articles.summary: Chen Jining's fall is part of the widest purge in the party's Politburo in several decades.
articles.full_text:
Image source, Getty Images Image caption, 
Chen Jining was a rising star in the Chinese Communist Party By Koh Ewe 
- Published 25 November 2026 
Chinese authorities are investigating Shanghai's party chief, a rising star in the Communist Party, as part of Xi Jinping's sweeping anti-corruption drive. 
Chen Jining, 62, is suspected of "severe violations of discipline and laws", according to a statement published on Tuesday by the party's anti-corruption body. 
Chen is now the fourth member of the elite Politburo to be investigated, in the widest purge yet of the party's top executive body since the end of the Cultural Revolution. 
As the party prepares to appoint fresh leaders at next year's National People's Congress, uncertainty looms over what its new command will look like - except that Xi will remain at the helm. 
Before Chen, three other members of the current Politburo - appointed in 2022 - were investigated and subsequently expelled: ex-generals He Weidong and Zhang Youxia, as well as former Xinjiang party chief Ma Xingrui. 
While Chen has not been removed from the Politburo, it's rare for officials to return after such investigations. 
"Who on this Politburo feels safe, especially as the personnel machinations for next year's Party Congress intensify?" China analyst Bill Bishop wrote in his Sinocism newsletter. 
Chen's investigation came as a surprise, according to Bishop, given rumours were swirling that another senior official, not Chen, would fall next in the anti-corruption campaign. 
The role of Shanghai party chief, which Chen assumed in 2022, is known to be a prestigious springboard to the country's top office. 
Chen's long list of predecessors include former president Jiang Zemin, his premier Zhu Rongji, incumbent premier Li Qiang and Xi Jinping himself. 
As Shanghai party chief, Chen hosted foreign leaders visiting the city, including former UK Prime Minister Keir Starmer in January and former US Secretary of State Antony Blinken in 2024. 
Chen was also a prominent champion for the development of the city's artificial intelligence industry - a sector that the party has stipulated as an area of strategic focus. 
Chen graduated with a degree in environmental engineering at Tsinghua University, where he returned to teach in 1998 and became its president in 2012. He also spent a few years in the UK, and received a PhD from Imperial College London. 
Since Xi's anti-corruption drive in 2012, more than two million individuals have been disciplined for cases related to "pointless formalities, bureaucratism, hedonism and extravagance", according to the party. 
Specific charges are often not made public, and broad allegations about disciplinary and legal violations have become routine in the crackdown. 
Analysts note that corruption also extends to ideological impurity - or simply put, disloyalty. 
Party discipline took centre stage at the fifth plenum last month, which had the most empty seats ever seen after a record 33 members were expelled from the party's central committee. 
Chen's ongoing probe suggests that the crackdown is not slowing down. 
Shanghai's communist party standing committee said in a statement that its members "unanimously expressed their firm support" for the decision of the party. 
The investigation of Chen, the committee said, shows that "the fight against corruption will not stop".

articles.title: What Jensen Huang's return teaches China's Xi about Trump
articles.summary: Huang being back at the helm of Nvidia is no guarantee of relief for Beijing.
articles.full_text:
Figure caption, 
A comeback for the ages: Trump's influence on Huang's return to Nvidia By Laura Bicker China correspondent 
- Published 24 November 2026 
Jensen Huang's reinstatement as Nvidia CEO has riveted the world - including China, where it has become the top trending post on Weibo, the country's biggest social media platform. 
Most users are pleased to see the return of the influential billionaire, who declared that he loved China, before videos appeared online of him eating noodles and drinking milk tea during a visit in May. Some wondered why - in the video of him returning to Nvidia's headquarters - he is not wearing one of his leather jackets. 
But to many, Huang's return, which is being dubbed one of the greatest U-turns of all time, seems like a vindication for China. 
That's probably how Xi Jinping sees it too. 
Beijing has dismissed claims that one of the women who had an affair with Jensen Huang had been recruited by China's Ministry of State Security, its version of the CIA, as a spy. Chinese state media has also framed the spy saga as a smear campaign orchestrated by China hawks in Washington. The Global Times, a Communist Party mouthpiece, described it as a "witch hunt". 
Now the White House, and President Donald Trump himself, have said Huang poses no national security threat, although investigations into the spy allegations are still ongoing. 
Image source, Getty Images Image caption, 
Trunmp and Xi ahead of their meeting in Shenzhen last week 
Xi will have learned many lessons from this scandal, especially about Trump's pressure points. 
For one, the fact that Huang's reappointment came so soon after Xi's meetings last week with Trump in Shenzhen could be read as a sign that direct engagement is an effective way to influence Washington. 
Trump has said the two men discussed Huang, but did not elaborate further. Beijing has not commented. 
The episode has also reinforced the view among Chinese officials that there are two camps in Washington: those in favour of restricting Chinese access to cutting edge tech to protect US national security, and those, like Huang, who believe that such restrictions will not limit Beijing's ambitions. 
Huang has repeatedly argued that US export controls will force Chinese firms like Huawei to build independent alternatives - all the while shutting American companies out of the world's second-largest economy. 
But him being back at the helm of Nvidia is no guarantee of relief for Beijing. 
Rather, the sale of advanced chips will remain a key point of contention between the US and China, especially as the two sides try to reach a trade deal before another Trump-Xi meeting, which is expected in December. 
Already new rules are being put in place that will worry Beijing. 
The US Bureau of Industry and Security is tightening restrictions by targeting not only the direct export of advanced chips to China, but also Chinese firms' ability to use computing power in data centres overseas. 
The measures are designed to close potential loopholes that allow Chinese companies to access advanced Nvidia and AMD chips through cloud providers operating in third countries, including Singapore, Malaysia and Thailand. 
China has yet to react with measures of its own. But investors will be watching closely for any escalation which could weigh on US equity markets. 
Image source, Getty Images Image caption, 
Jensen Huang at an Nvidia event in Berlin in October 
And having seen how eager Trump is to keep things stable, Xi may see this as leverage. 
He now knows Trump is so worried about the stock market that he is prepared to intervene in the HR decisions of the world's biggest company. The president has also personally invested in Nvidia, although the White House has emphasised that Trump has placed his businesses in a trust managed by his sons. 
China has already used its considerable chokehold over the world's rare earth metals to bring the US to the negotiating table over trade. 
If Washington restricts chip exports and Beijing retaliates, that could be the start of a cycle that has a profound effect on the stock market because American companies, from car makers to defence firms to chip manufacturers, all rely on rare earths. 
What China has realised is that more trouble lies ahead as it tries to build what it describes as a "constructive strategic relationship" with the US. 
Trump's tariffs are no longer at the heart of that tussle. Now it's about control of critical technology and minerals which could, in turn, affect each side's military influence and economic power. 
What happens next will depend on how the Jensen Huang saga unfolds because it is far from over. 
Huang is set to testify before Congress next month, and come January, a Democrat-controlled Congress will raise the pressure. Even some Republican lawmakers have made clear they want answers. 
Arkansas senator Tom Cotton wrote on X that the Nvidia controversy "is just the tip of the iceberg and it's not resolved because Jensen Huang has his job back".

articles.title: Is China behind a wave of AI fake videos targeting Taiwan?
articles.summary: The network attacked key figures in the ruling DPP, including President Lai and mayoral candidate Shen.
articles.full_text:
By Sam Howarth   and   Matt Murphy ,  BBC Verify 
- Published 24 November 2026 
Taiwan's ruling party is being repeatedly targeted with AI videos spreading false claims about its leader and other key members ahead of crucial local elections, BBC Verify has found. 
A China-linked network has pumped out more than 500 fake videos about the Democratic Progressive Party (DPP) in the past year, which experts suggest is part of a long-running campaign to influence the outcome of the elections. 
The videos appear to try to smear President Lai Ching-te by claiming he holds a US green card - and would abandon Taiwan if war broke out with China - which Taiwan's presidential office says is completely false. Deepfakes also appear to show Puma Shen, who is running to be the mayor of capital Taipei, using drugs, which he denies. Others seek to undermine or ridicule the politicians by showing them in children's clothing or as popular film characters. 
The Taipei mayoralty has traditionally served as a springboard to the presidency. Experts say this has made Shen, who has been openly critical of Beijing, an obvious target for disinformation campaigns. The current mayor, Chiang Wan-an, is part of Taiwan's Kuomintang (KMT) party, which favours closer ties with China. 
Taiwan is a self-governing island that China claims as part of its territory. Beijing and Taipei have long observed an uneasy status quo under which Taiwan, backed by the US, neither formally declares independence nor unites with China. 
But tensions have risen since the DPP came to power in 2016. Beijing has repeatedly accused the party of pursuing independence while China's leader Xi Jinping, who has said "reunification" with Taiwan is a key goal, has stepped up pressure against the party with increased military activity around the island. 
Experts believe the current disinformation activity is part of a broader campaign against Taiwan designed to undermine trust in its democratic process. 
Image caption, 
The campaign has targeted Taiwan's President Lai (top) and his predecessor Tsai (bottom) 
"The account operators are trying to make people distrust the DPP politicians so that they will not believe whatever they say," Austin Horng-En Wang, an expert in cognitive warfare at the University of Nevada, Las Vegas, told BBC Verify. "If you don't trust that candidate then you will not listen to what they say," he added. 
The videos, many of which were shared from an account called "noxparable" or carried a watermark with the same name, have been viewed tens of millions of times across several social media platforms since May 2025. 
More than half of those views were tracked in the past four months as the activity has ramped up ahead of the elections. Many of the accounts involved in spreading disinformation listed their locations on social media as mainland China and Hong Kong, while a number of the clips carried labels showing they were generated with AI. Many people who engaged with the videos were often seen repeating the false claims or attacking DPP figures in the comments, while others appeared to treat the clips as entertainment. 
One of the most widely shared videos targeted Shen by superimposing his face onto a man who is seen holding a lighter and exhaling smoke alongside claims he is smoking drugs. The video appears to build on accusations from Taiwan's opposition party that he supports drugs decriminalisation, which Shen denies, and was debunked by a local news network. 
Shen has taken legal action against people sharing deepfakes, local media reported, while his campaign office said AI videos showing the candidate appeared to be part of a "classic tactic China uses to smear specific targets". BBC Verify contacted the Chinese embassy in London for comment and did not receive a reply, but China has previously denied accusations of electoral interference. 
Image caption, 
Many of the fake videos ridiculed President Lai and Shen while others portrayed other KMT candidates such as Ko Chih-en (above) in a positive light 
Other debunked claims include allegations that Lai's predecessor Tsai Ing-wen had fraudulently obtained her PhD from the London School of Economics. The university pushed back on identical allegations in 2019 and confirmed it had awarded her the doctorate. 
A number of the social media accounts BBC Verify identified as sharing the disinformation videos appeared to be linked to Chinese firm Borderless, which produces websites that blend apolitical content with pro-China messaging. The network has also been investigated by journalists at the Taiwanese independent media outlet The Reporter, who shared their findings with BBC Verify. Borderless has previously been accused of carrying out "cognitive warfare" against Taiwan by Taipei's National Security Bureau. BBC Verify contacted the firm for comment but did not receive a reply. 
Analysts confirmed to BBC Verify there were also linguistic clues that the accounts, which presented themselves as based in Taiwan, were actually posting from China. The posts occasionally used a simplified Chinese script introduced by the Communist government which was never adopted in Taiwan. 
The posts mostly appeared during regular office hours, which Wang suggested showed a "professional" operation, while the accounts originating outside Taiwan showed evidence of election interfering. "When they pretended to be citizens in another country and used these accounts to manipulate the public opinion of the other country during the campaign, it is definitely election interference," Wang added. 
Earlier this month, Taiwan's central election commission aired an advert warning voters to "beware of AI-generated deepfake videos" circulating online that could seek to influence the upcoming election. It comes as government officials flagged nearly 2,700 social media accounts to Meta that it claimed were part of a Chinese information warfare campaign, Reuters reported. Meta said it had removed the accounts. 
Andrew Yeh of the China Strategic Risk Institute said the ultimate goal is not to favour any party. "China's information operations succeed not just by backing one candidate or opposing another, but by diluting Taiwan's policy debates, driving polarisation and degrading Taiwanese citizens' trust in their democratic processes," he said. 
"Regardless of whether the KMT or DPP comes out on top, a more fractured and more divided Taiwan is in Beijing's interests."

articles.title: The Indian 'Tamasha queen' whose fans paid for a show that never happened
articles.summary: A new Bollywood flim spotlights the remarkable life of dancer and singer Vithabhai Narayangaonkar.
articles.full_text:
Image source, Pradnya Daya Pawar Image caption, 
Vithabhai Narayangaonkar was a legend in Maharashtra's folk theatre By Amrita Kadam ,  BBC Marathi   and   Zoya Mateen ,  BBC News, Delhi 
- Published 2 hours ago 
Few things could keep Vithabai Narayangaonkar, one of the greatest stars of Maharashtra's folk theatre, away from the stage. 
Not even, it would seem, the birth of her child. 
In the 1960s, the singer, dancer and troupe leader was performing in Shikhar Shingnapur, a village in the western Indian state, when she went into labour. 
"She quietly stepped behind the stage into a makeshift tent while the rest of us continued performing," her daughter, veteran folk artist Mangala Bansode, told BBC Marathi. 
Outside, the restless audience kept shouting: "Where is Vitha?" 
When Vithabai returned to the stage, she was cradling her newborn son, the seventh of her eight children. 
"The audience was stunned, but they quietly left, saying, 'We will watch your performance later'," Bansode recalled. 
Outspoken and quick-witted, Vithabai held audiences across Maharashtra in thrall for decades, earning the title of Tamasha Samradnyi – the empress of Tamasha, the state's traditional travelling folk theatre. 
Now, more than two decades after her death, her life has inspired a Bollywood musical, Eetha, starring Shraddha Kapoor, and due for release on 4 December. 
Directed by Laxman Utekar, Eetha is based on Yogiraj Bagul's Marathi book chronicling Vithabai's life. 
Rooted in devotional poetry, Tamasha evolved into a lively mix of music, dance, comedy and drama. At its heart is Lavani, a song and dance tradition in which verses ranging from the bawdy to the politically incisive are performed to the beat of the dholki, a percussion instrument. 
Eetha evokes the world of Tamasha in its heyday. Kapoor, who had never performed Lavani before, learnt to dance while wearing musical anklets weighing 4kg each. 
"The lives of Tamasha artists have been very tough, so in their dance you see pain as well as joy," Kapoor recalled at a promotional event. 
Image source, Getty Images Image caption, 
Eetha hits the theatres on 5 December 
Many Tamasha performers, including Vithabai, came from oppressed castes, facing discrimination even as their artistry drew large crowds. 
How much of that history Eetha will capture remains debated. Utekar says it is not a biopic, but his decision to rename the protagonist Vithabai Bhau Gavkar instead of Vithabai Bhau Mang Narayangaonkar has drawn criticism. 
For critics, much of Vithabai's history was contained in her name – Mang identified her with a historically oppressed Dalit community, while Narayangaonkar spoke of her family's roots in Narayangaon village. Both featured in the name of the troupe she inherited from her father – Bhau-Bapu Mang Narayangaonkar Tamasha Mandal. 
Vithabai spoke openly about caste and the indignities Tamasha artists faced, themes that also surfaced in her songs. In a 1960s Lavani documented by historian Shailaja Paik, she rebuked men for lewd gestures, reminding them she danced to earn a living, not to please them. 
It was a livelihood she had inherited from generations of performers in her family. 
Like her son, Vithabai was born during a Tamasha performance, in 1935. Her mother, Shanta, had continued touring with her husband Bhau's troupe throughout her pregnancy. 
Vithabai joined a theatre group at eight and her father's troupe at 13, soon becoming its star. After her father and co-leader Bapu died in quick succession, she took over the troupe with her husband and cousin. 
Her career flourished during Tamasha's golden age, when productions grew more elaborate, drawing on mythology, history and contemporary life, says folk arts scholar Sukhada Khandge. 
Khandge, who watched Vithabai perform as a child, recalls her sparkling eyes and commanding presence. She was as expressive with her face as she was with her feet. 
Image source, Pradnya Daya Pawar Image caption, 
Vithabai was known as the empress of Tamasha in Maharashtra 
Her fame carried her beyond Maharashtra. 
During India's war with China in 1962, Vithabai performed for soldiers in the North-East Frontier Agency, now largely Arunachal Pradesh, braving freezing conditions just three months after giving birth, Bansode says. 
At a conference in 1996, she recalled meeting soldiers from the historically oppressed Mahar and Mang communities at the frontier. 
"Our Mahar-Mang soldiers were expected to fight and lay down their lives defending the nation, but the very same people would not even allow our bridegroom to pass through the village entrance," she said. 
Despite offers from leading filmmakers, including Raj Kapoor, and roles in Marathi cinema, Vithabai refused to leave theatre. Film fame, she felt, would benefit her alone, while her troupe supported some 50 families, Bansode says. 
There was a tenderness, too, in her relationship with audiences. 
In his book on Vithabai's life, which inspired Eetha, Yogiraj Bagul recounts a performance in Mumbai during Diwali in 1971. 
Despite the threat of rain, spectators insisted on buying tickets, saying the money would be their Bhau Beej gift to Vithabai if the show was cancelled – a festival celebrating the bond between brothers and sisters. 
When the rain came, people left chanting: "Bhau Beej, Bhau Beej." 
No one asked for their money back. 
But Vithabai's fortunes failed to match her fame. Her husband, Maruti Sawant, mismanaged the troupe's finances and took loans in her name, family members say. By the time she left him in 1982, she was heavily indebted. 
Bagul also writes about a 1986 column in a Marathi daily that revealed how the empress of Tamasha was now travelling on public buses and staying in cheap accommodation. 
Image source, Getty Images Image caption, 
Despite drawing huge crowds, Lavni dancers were often disdained 
Despite public support, Vithabai was forced to disband her troupe in 1990 – the same year she received the Sangeet Natak Akademi Award, one of India's highest performing arts honours. 
Vithabai successfully campaigned for government pensions for Tamasha artists. But many of the hardships she knew persist today, says Marathi writer Pradnya Daya Pawar. 
Troupes spend nearly eight months a year on the road, with performers struggling to feed their children and educate them, she says. Despite government aid, many remain indebted to private moneylenders. 
Vithabai's financial struggles persisted until her death in January 2002. Her family could pay only 4,000 of the 5,900 rupees owed to the Pune hospital where she died, the Times of India reported. 
Fellow artists and admirers chipped in to bring her body home to Narayangaon. 
Maharashtra has since instituted a lifetime achievement award in her name. 
Eetha could now introduce Vithabai to a generation that never saw her perform, though the changes to her name have left some uneasy. 
Marathi writer Pragya Daya Pawar argues that omitting the reference to Vithabai's caste risks obscuring the difficulties she confronted. 
"It erases the social location, struggle and resistance that shaped her remarkable journey, reducing an extraordinary artist's story to a purely individual achievement," she says. 
But Bansode, who spent years performing alongside her mother, says there is much to celebrate. 
"The name doesn't matter to me. I am simply proud that a film is being made about my mother," she says.
